findings.title: Removing the multiple-provider error makes provider selection silent and non-deterministic on order ties
findings.body: detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath. Now it just sorts by order() and takes the first, logging the rest at debug level. All three real providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) return the same order value of 200, so if two of them ever end up on the same classpath (e.g. keycloak-crypto-default accidentally present in a FIPS deployment) the selection depends purely on ServiceLoader iteration order and the deployment silently runs with the wrong crypto stack (non-FIPS BouncyCastle instead of BCFIPS) instead of failing fast. Either keep a hard failure for equal-order providers, or give the providers distinct orders and log the ignored ones at WARN.

findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: order() is added to the public CryptoProvider SPI interface without a default implementation. Any third-party or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider (including the copies maintained in the keycloak-client repository) will no longer compile and will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError after upgrading. Adding `default int order() { return 100; }` (or some documented baseline) would keep the SPI backward compatible.

findings.title: logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as the format
findings.body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a runtime-built message as the format string with no arguments. If any provider class name ever contains a '%' (or the message is changed later) the formatting throws/produces garbage inside logging. Also the message is concatenated unconditionally even when debug logging is disabled, and it ends with a dangling ", ". Use `logger.debugf("Ignored crypto providers: %s", ...)` with the joined names instead.

findings.title: Malformed ASN.1 input causes unchecked exceptions instead of IOException
findings.body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length encoding (0x80) and can return 0. readInteger() then calls read(length) with that value: read(-1) allocates `new byte[-1]` and throws NegativeArraySizeException, and for length 0 `new BigInteger(new byte[0])` throws NumberFormatException. Both are unchecked exceptions escaping methods declared to throw IOException, so an attacker-supplied/corrupted ECDSA signature propagates an unexpected runtime exception to callers of asn1derToConcatenatedRS instead of a handled IOException. Validate length > 0 and reject indefinite-length encodings with an IOException.

findings.title: Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write rBigInteger/sBigInteger into them and discard the results; the actual DER output is built from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect (only wasted allocations) and are confusing to readers; they should be removed.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider, not a BC provider
findings.body: The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically the JDK SUN provider. BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER is initialized from this method's return value and is then used as the provider name in provider-specific lookups elsewhere in keycloak-core (Signature.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER) etc.). With this provider installed, those lookups resolve against SUN and can fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException for algorithms only offered by BC, which is hard to diagnose. It also instantiates a KeyStore on every call just to read a provider. Returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or caching an explicit provider reference would be clearer.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests use a 256-bit EC key and only round-trip the new code against itself
findings.body: The key pair is generated with the default EC curve (P-256) and reused for ES384 and ES512, so r/s are always ~32 bytes and the 48/66-byte component paths of integerToBytes/concatenatedRSToASN1DER are never exercised with realistic values. In addition the test only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS is self-consistent; it never verifies the produced DER/concatenated bytes against a known-good encoding or against the existing BC-based ECDSACryptoProvider, so an encoding bug that is symmetric in both directions would pass. Generate P-256/P-384/P-521 keys per algorithm and assert the DER signature verifies with java.security.Signature (or compare with the BC implementation output).

findings.title: No test covers the new provider-selection ordering logic
findings.body: detectProvider() changed from fail-fast on multiple providers to order-based selection, which is the core behavioural change of this PR (the Keycloak testsuite now has both DefaultCryptoProvider and AuthzClientCryptoProvider on the classpath). There is no unit test asserting that the higher-order provider wins, that the list is correctly sorted, or what happens when the orders are equal, so a regression in this selection (silently picking the wrong crypto provider) would go unnoticed.
